diagnose-outputs.summary: Work out why a prompt or configuration is producing poor output by checking, in order, the prompt itself, the context and knowledge available, the request size, the conversation length, and where the chat actually lives.
points: Generic output almost always means a generic prompt: no audience, no purpose, no required content, no length or format. The fix is to state who the output is for, what it must cover, and how it should look.
Identical outputs across different inputs (a shared 'generator' prompt) mean missing context and missing examples. Add the specific inputs each run and one or two examples of what good looks like.
Vague quality adjectives ('compelling', 'specific', 'creative') and capitalised 'MUST' do not supply missing information; they are the tempting non-fix.
Wrong format: if you needed a table with particular columns, a bullet list, or a fixed structure, say so explicitly; regenerating and hoping is not a diagnosis.
Overloaded requests (five tasks in one message) produce shallow results on all of them. Split into sequential requests and check each before continuing.

Stale Project knowledge produces confident, outdated answers. When a Project consistently quotes old prices, procedures or policies, check the knowledge files before touching instructions or model; replace superseded files and remove the old ones.

Project instructions and knowledge apply only to chats started inside the Project. A chat opened from the main page with a manual attachment has none of that configuration, however the instructions are worded.

Very long conversations degrade: contradictions, forgotten decisions and slower replies. Length limits are set by the context window per conversation; the remedy is a fresh chat that opens with a written summary of decisions and constraints.
Length limits (how long one conversation can be) are different from usage limits (how much you can use Claude across all chats in a period); a plan upgrade does not fix a diluted conversation.
Switching to a bigger model is rarely the diagnosis; a more capable model still cannot know facts that are absent from the prompt or the knowledge.
'Remember everything above' and self-check instructions are not remedies for context dilution or calculation errors; structural fixes (restart, split, verify) are.

adjust-approach.summary: Change the right thing in response to results: give specific feedback on a draft, add or diversify examples, add constraints, split the task, or switch feature or model when the prompt is not the problem.
points: When a draft is close but off in tone, length or emphasis, reply with precise feedback naming what to keep and what to change; do not restart from scratch or accept the poor fit.

Examples raise quality but the model copies them. If outputs become uniform (same structure, same offer for every case), diversify the example set and state what the examples illustrate (tone, structure) versus what varies.
Removing all examples after over-fitting returns you to the weaker state; adding more of the same example makes over-copying worse.
Add explicit constraints when outputs are too long, miss required elements or drift: required sections, maximum length, forbidden content. Constraints work better than adjectives.

When an early step's errors (data cleaning, calculations) contaminate later steps (narrative, slides), decompose the work and insert a verification point after the step that matters; regenerating downstream content alone reproduces the errors.

Recognise when the prompt is not the problem. Questions needing current, cited facts require web search or research mode; a bigger model, 'use the latest information', or format examples cannot supply information the model does not have.

Switch model when the task's demands changed: a faster, lower-cost model for high-volume, straightforward work; a more capable model for deep reasoning. Switching models is not a fix for missing context.

Iterate systematically: define success criteria before changing anything, test each version on the same representative inputs, change one element at a time, and keep a version log so you can return to a known-good prompt.
Model self-ratings are not a quality measure; your own criteria and human review are. Separate personal copies of a shared prompt destroy consistency.
Fixing one complaint and causing another on each revision is the signature of iterating without fixed criteria and a fixed test set.

optimize-workflows.summary: Make recurring Claude work faster and more reliable with Projects, shared templates and saved prompts, well-placed human review checkpoints, and curated knowledge, without trading away quality.
points: Re-pasting the same instructions, style guide or reference material every chat is the signal to create a Project: its instructions and knowledge persist across conversations and updates happen in one place.
A single never-ending conversation is not a substitute for a Project; it degrades, hits the length limit and mixes unrelated work.
A new chat cannot see earlier chats unless a feature (Projects, memory) supplies the content; 'remember last week' does not work on its own.

When several people do the same task with different personal prompts, inconsistency follows. Centralise the template, rules and examples in a shared Project with a standard prompt that takes the variable inputs.

Standardised output formats (fixed sections, fixed scoring) make runs fast, comparable and easy to review; they also let you direct human attention to exceptions (scores that changed or fell below threshold).

Place a human review checkpoint at the point of highest consequence (before content reaches clients, the public or a decision), with a short checklist focused on what has gone wrong before. This keeps most of the time saving while making the output trustworthy.
'Double-check your figures' inside the prompt is a weak safeguard; a person checking figures against the source is the reliable one. Reverting to fully manual work is the over-correction.
Never remove the human from external communications with commercial or personal consequences to save a few minutes; review by exception is fine, no review is not.

Project knowledge is loaded with each chat, so a bloated knowledge base with superseded files costs speed and usage and produces stale citations. Curate: remove old versions, keep current documents, add an index that says which file is authoritative.
Claude cannot modify Project knowledge from inside a conversation; a person must add, replace or remove files.

Usage-limit hygiene: shorter focused conversations, starting new chats for new topics, trimming attachments to what is needed, and using the right model for the job all stretch usage further than a plan upgrade alone.
Escalate when an optimisation needs automation beyond the app (API integrations, agents, connectors to internal systems): that is Claude Architect and Developer territory.
